new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's fixed: final syllable rule for the native sesquisyllabic (minor-disyllable) class: presyllable unstressed, main syllable stressed. Adds the qualification that this is stated only for minor disyllables; major disyllables are treated as two full syllables without a stress statement, and polysyllabic loans are not covered, so the catalog's extension to 3-8 syllable words is not supported by this source. The listed open_url (wals.info/refdb/record/1278) is the wrong item (it is Innes 1964 on Loko) and the Cambridge DOI is paywalled (extract only); the open copy used is the archive.org Digital Library of India scan of the whole volume.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Native words are monosyllables or disyllables. In 'minor disyllables' (a reduced presyllable with restricted vowel and obligatory nasal final, plus a full major syllable) stress falls on the second, final syllable and the first syllable is unstressed relative to it; the two-pattern table on p. 170 labels the minor disyllable '(Lack of Stress) (Stress)'. Major disyllables (two full syllables) are said to be pronounced in isolation as a succession of two monosyllables, with no relative stress stated. Nothing is said about stress in the small class of Pali/Sanskrit polysyllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Major disyllables (e.g. pontae 'however', kambət 'knife', piba:k 'difficult') are described as two full monosyllables with no stress asymmetry stated; polysyllables of Pali/Sanskrit origin are literary and get no stress statement; in rapid speech minor disyllables reduce to extended monosyllables (e.g. konlah > [kəlah]). The description is of one speaker, Keng Vannsak (born Kompong Chhnang), checked with Keo Mongkry.
new_statements.identity_note: Henderson 1952 describes the speech of one Cambodian speaker, Keng Vannsak, born at Kompong Chhnang, checked against Keo Mongkry (Central Khmer of Cambodia). Wichitkhachee 1996 (not opened) is titled as a study of the Khmer spoken at Ban Nawattai, Chachoengsao province, Thailand, an enclave variety. Ungsitipoonporn 2001 (not opened) is about Chong (Pearic), Khlong Phlu and Wang Kraprae, not Khmer, despite its PuRe ISO tag.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every clause of the deciding quotation is on the page images we hold of Huffman 1970:11-12 (running heads verified), and the supporting p.104 and p.4 lines are in the text we hold layer; Nacaskul 1978:189 image matches the secondary quote. (2) The deciding work is a 1970 pedagogical reader, but its phonology section is by the field's specialist and is corroborated by a 1978 phonology article; all sources seen (Huffman, Nacaskul, Butler 2014) agree that presyllables/minor syllables are unstressed and the word-final full syllable stressed, and Huffman's own polysyllable grids (1011, 11101) support the shape-not-count reading, so nothing in hand suggests the weight-hedged/right-edge coding is wrong. (3) It is not the best available: Henderson 1952, Huffman 1972 (Lingua), Huffman 1970 MSC pp.10-11 (the StressTyp2 locus, reportedly with an explicit secondary-stress placement rule)

sources.quote: p.66: 'both the MCVE of extended monosyllables and the nucleus of minor syllables are unstressed'; Fig. 2.4 transcribes a minor disyllable as [khʌm.ˈkhat] (final stress); p.9 (defining property of sesquisyllables): 'prosodic prominence (i.e. stress or tone) must be word-final'. Adopts Henderson's 1952 four word types (simple/extended monosyllable, minor/major disyllable). Instrumental content concerns cluster underlap/minor-syllable vocoids, not stress placement in major disyllables or polysyllables.
